diagnosis.root_cause: The test blocks in GenericTestUtils.waitFor polling for a DelegationTokenRenewer background-thread timeout / token-removal condition that is driven by wall-clock scheduling and Thread.sleep, and it is bounded by JUnit's 30s @Test timeout. Under CI load the renewer thread's sleep/scheduling and the polling loop's sleep race, so the expected state is never observed before the 30s deadline and the test times out.

evidence.why: The failure stack shows the test is parked inside GenericTestUtils.waitFor (which calls Thread.sleep) at this line, i.e. it is polling for a timing-dependent condition rather than failing on an assertion.

The Renewer returns absolute expiry times computed from System.currentTimeMillis(), so whether the renewer thread wakes and expires the token before the test's 30s deadline depends on real elapsed time and thread scheduling, which is inherently flaky under load.

The 30s JUnit timeout is a hard wall-clock bound; when the sleep-based waitFor loop plus renewer-thread scheduling exceed it (slow machine, GC, contention), the test is aborted with TestTimedOutException exactly as observed.

history.hypothesis: The nested BoxOfFoo class keeps a static `iterations` counter that is never reset, so if the JUnitQuickcheck run happens more than once in the same JVM the counter accumulates (e.g. 200 instead of 100), breaking assertEquals; running the test back-to-back in the same JVM will expose this leaked static state.

diagnosis.root_cause: The test class BoxOfFoo keeps its trial counter in a static field `iterations` that is never reset, so each time the test class is executed in the same JVM the counter accumulates (100, then 200, then 300). When the harness runs the test more than once in the same JVM, boxOfFoo's assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), BoxOfFoo.iterations) sees the stale accumulated value (300) instead of a fresh 100 and fails.

evidence.why: `iterations` is a static field of the nested BoxOfFoo class and is never reset between executions; running the enclosing test a second/third time in the same JVM accumulates 100 per run, so the assertion reads 200/300 rather than 100.

Line 45 asserts equality between the fresh trial count (100) and the accumulated static counter; because the counter is incremented once per trial per run and never cleared, the assertion fails with expected:<100> but was:<300> on the third same-JVM execution, matching the reproduced failure.

history.hypothesis: The nested PrimitiveBytes class keeps non-resettable static state (`iterations` and `values`), so if the test body is executed more than once in the same JVM the trial-count assertion (and possibly the subList(0,2) check) breaks, making the test order/re-run dependent.

diagnosis.root_cause: The PrimitiveBytes fixture keeps mutable static state (`static int iterations` and `static final List<Byte> values`) that is never reset. When the test method runs a second time in the same JVM, the property is executed again and both the trial counter and value list accumulate, so `PrimitiveBytes.iterations` becomes 200 instead of the expected default trial count of 100.

evidence.why: This is the failing call site (line 119) that asserts iterations == 100 but observes 200 because the static counter was left over from a previous run in the same JVM.

Neither `iterations` nor `values` is reset between executions; each property trial increments iterations and appends to values, so a second in-JVM execution doubles the count to 200 and shifts the subList seen by the test.

history.hypothesis: The test is not idempotent: static fields (iterations and values) in the nested PrimitiveDoubles class accumulate across runs in the same JVM, so a second run in the same JVM causes iteration count and value list assertions to fail.

diagnosis.root_cause: The primitiveDoubles test fails on its second execution in the same JVM: the static counter PrimitiveDoubles.iterations is only incremented by the property (++iterations) and is never reset to 0 after the test, unlike sibling tests such as primitiveBooleans and primitiveBytes which end with `iterations = 0`. The property runs defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100) times per execution, so on the second run in the same JVM the static field has accumulated to 200, and the assertion at ExhaustingAGivenSetButIncludingAnotherTest.java:209 (expected:<100> but was:<200>) fails.

evidence.why: This is the failing test method; unlike the sibling tests it lacks a trailing `PrimitiveDoubles.iterations = 0;` reset. The assertion at line 209 compares the static iterations against 100, and on a second in-JVM run the static field still holds the previous run's total, yielding 200. The stack trace confirms the failure is at this file line 209.

`iterations` is a static field that the property increments on every trial; because it is process-wide (not per-execution) and is never cleared, state persists across repeated test runs in the same JVM, which is exactly the non-idempotent-outcome mechanism.

Sibling tests explicitly reset their static iteration counter after asserting, showing that the reset is the intended invariant that primitiveDoubles omits; without it the counter doubles to 200 on the second run.

diagnosis.root_cause: The nested @RunWith(JUnitQuickcheck.class) class WrapperChars keeps its counters in static fields (`iterations` and `values`) that are never reset between runs. JUnitQuickcheck invokes the property defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100) times, so on the first execution the counter reaches 100, but when the same test class is executed again in the same JVM (subrun 1 of the 2-run strategy) the static counter accumulates to 200, making assertEquals(100, WrapperChars.iterations) fail with 'expected:<100> but was:<200>'. The failure is therefore an artifact of re-running the test in the same JVM against mutated static state, not of the property itself.

evidence.why: Line 185 is exactly the frame in the failure stack (SamplingButAlsoIncludingAGivenSetTest.java:185). It asserts the static counter equals defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100); on the second in-JVM execution the counter has accumulated to 200, producing the observed AssertionError.

`iterations` (and `values`) are static mutable state shared across all runs of the test in the same JVM. Because JUnitQuickcheck re-invokes shouldHold defaultPropertyTrialCount() times per run, the counter never resets, so a second execution in the same JVM pushes it from 100 to 200 and breaks the assertion at line 185.
